bigPicture.subtitle: Christ Is All — and You Are Complete in Him
bigPicture.thesis: If we had to summarize the Book of Colossians in one overarching thought, it is this: Jesus Christ is supreme over everything, and because all the fullness of God dwells in Him, you need nothing added to Him. You are complete in Christ — so set your mind on Him, and live every part of life in His name.
paragraphs: Start with the problem, because Paul did. Colossae was a small, fading town in the Lycus valley, overshadowed by its wealthier neighbours Laodicea and Hierapolis. Paul had never visited it. The church had been planted by Epaphras, one of their own, who had heard the gospel from Paul in Ephesus and carried it home. Now Epaphras had come to Paul in prison with good news and bad news. The good news was their faith and love. The bad news was a teaching that sounded deeply spiritual: a mixture of human philosophy, Jewish food laws and festivals, worship of angels, visions, and harsh treatment of the body. It did not deny Christ. It simply said Christ was not enough.

Paul's answer is the highest view of Christ in all his letters. Before he says a word about the false teaching, he sings a hymn: Christ “is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of all creation” (1:15). “For by him all things were created, in the heavens and on the earth, things visible and things invisible, whether thrones or dominions or principalities or powers; all things have been created through him, and for him” (1:16). “He is before all things, and in him all things are held together” (1:17). He is the Creator, the Sustainer, the Head of the church, the firstborn from the dead, the Reconciler of all things, “that in all things he might have the preeminence” (1:18). If He is this great, what could anyone add to Him?

That is exactly the argument of chapter 2. “For in him all the fullness of the Deity dwells bodily, and in him you are made full” (2:9–10). Believers have been circumcised in Him, buried and raised with Him, made alive and forgiven. The record of debt against them has been cancelled: “he has taken it out of the way, nailing it to the cross” (2:14). The powers the false teachers feared have been defeated: “having stripped the principalities and the powers, he made a show of them openly, triumphing over them in it” (2:15). So rules about food and festivals are only shadows; Christ is the substance. Human regulations look wise but cannot change the heart. The Colossians needed nothing more. They needed to go deeper into what they already had.

And then the letter turns to life. Because you were raised with Christ, “seek the things that are above, where Christ is, seated on the right hand of God” (3:1). Put off the old self and put on the new, clothed in compassion, kindness, humility, gentleness and patience, bound together by love. Let the peace of Christ rule, let His word dwell richly, and “Whatever you do, in word or in deed, do all in the name of the Lord Jesus” (3:17). That reaches into marriage, parenting and daily work, into prayer, speech to outsiders and friendships in ministry. The supreme Christ of chapter 1 becomes the Lord of the kitchen, the workshop and the conversation. That is Colossians: Christ is all, and in all.

map.intro: Colossians is the twelfth book of the New Testament and one of Paul's four “prison letters,” alongside Ephesians, Philippians and Philemon. It was carried by Tychicus, together with Ephesians and the short letter to Philemon, and sent to a small church in the Lycus valley in the Roman province of Asia, about a hundred miles inland from Ephesus.

sections.title: The Twin of Ephesians
sections.body: Colossians and Ephesians were written at the same time, sent with the same messenger and share much of the same language: the old self and the new, Christ as Head of the body, the household codes, the psalms, hymns and spiritual songs. But they have different emphases. Ephesians focuses on the church, the body of Christ, and God's plan to unite all things in Him. Colossians focuses on Christ, the Head, and His absolute supremacy. Ephesians says, ‘be filled with the Spirit’; Colossians says, ‘let the word of Christ dwell in you richly’ — and both produce the same singing, thankful, submissive church. Read together, they show the Head and the body as one.

sections.title: After Philippians: From Christ's Descent to Christ's Throne
sections.body: Philippians showed Christ humbling Himself, taking the form of a servant and becoming obedient to death on a cross, and then being exalted to the name above every name. Colossians starts where that exaltation ends: with Christ as Creator and Sustainer of everything, the One in whom all fullness dwells. Philippians teaches believers to have the mind of Christ; Colossians teaches them that they are complete in Christ. Philippians is joy in Christ whatever the circumstances; Colossians is sufficiency in Christ whatever the competing teaching. Both were written from chains, and both put Christ at the centre of everything.

sections.title: A Letter for Every Generation of ‘Christ Plus’
sections.body: The exact mixture at Colossae has gone, but its shape keeps returning. Every generation produces teachings that do not deny Jesus but quietly add to Him: Christ plus a special experience, Christ plus a secret knowledge, Christ plus a diet or calendar, Christ plus spiritual techniques, Christ plus fear of spiritual powers. Colossians is the church's standing answer. It does not fight these ideas mainly by arguing against each detail. It fights them by showing Christ so clearly that additions look small. Whenever believers feel incomplete or anxious about the spiritual realm, Colossians says: look again at Him.

roadAhead.intro: The Road Ahead: Colossians ended with Christ enthroned at God's right hand and with the promise, “When Christ, our life, is revealed, then you will also be revealed with him in glory” (3:4). The next two books take that promise and look at it closely. 1 and 2 Thessalonians are letters about the return of Christ — how to live while waiting for Him, and how not to be shaken while He delays.

books.connection: Colossians lifted your eyes to where Christ is now; 1 Thessalonians lifts them to where He is coming from. It is one of Paul's earliest letters, written to a young church just months old, persecuted almost from the start. They had “turned to God from idols, to serve a living and true God” (1 Thessalonians 1:9), and now they waited “for his Son from heaven” (1 Thessalonians 1:10). But some of their members had died, and they were grieving: would those believers miss Christ's coming? Paul answers with one of the clearest passages on the return of Jesus: “For the Lord himself will descend from heaven with a shout, with the voice of the archangel, and with God’s trumpet. The dead in Christ will rise first” (1 Thessalonians 4:16), and then, “So we will be with the Lord forever” (1 Thessalonians 4:17). Colossians said your life is hidden with Christ; 1 Thessalonians tells you the day the hiding ends. And like Colossians, it turns hope into daily life: “Rejoice always. Pray without ceasing. In everything give thanks” (1 Thessalonians 5:16–18). Watch for how the hope of His coming produces holiness, love and work.

If Colossians warned against people adding to Christ, 2 Thessalonians warns against people confusing the church about Christ's return. Someone had told the Thessalonians, perhaps through a forged letter, that the day of the Lord had already come. Paul writes to steady them: “not to be quickly shaken in your mind, and not be troubled, either by spirit, or by word, or by letter as if from us, saying that the day of Christ has already come” (2 Thessalonians 2:2). Certain things must happen first, including “the rebellion” and the revealing of “the man of sin” (2 Thessalonians 2:3). Meanwhile some believers had stopped working, waiting idly for the end. Paul is blunt: “If anyone will not work, don’t let him eat” (2 Thessalonians 3:10). This echoes Colossians 3:23, where work is done heartily for the Lord. And he ends with encouragement: “But you, brothers, don’t be weary in doing what is right” (2 Thessalonians 3:13). Watch for how true hope makes believers steady, faithful and hard-working, not anxious or idle.

themesMastered.title: The Supremacy of Christ
themesMastered.body: “He is the head of the body, the assembly, who is the beginning, the firstborn from the dead; that in all things he might have the preeminence” (1:18). The hymn of 1:15–20 is the heart of the letter. Christ is the image of the invisible God: if you want to know what God is like, look at Jesus. He is the Creator of all things, including every throne and power in the unseen realm. He holds everything together right now. He is the Head of the church and the first to rise from the dead. Every other theme in Colossians flows from this one. Because He is supreme, nothing can rival Him, nothing needs to be added to Him, and every part of your life belongs to Him.

themesMastered.title: Complete in Christ
themesMastered.body: “For in him all the fullness of the Deity dwells bodily, and in him you are made full” (2:9–10). The false teachers said the Colossians were missing something. Paul says that in Christ they had everything. They were circumcised in Him with a circumcision not made with hands, buried and raised with Him, made alive and forgiven. Their spiritual growth would not come from going beyond Christ but from going deeper into Him: “As therefore you received Christ Jesus, the Lord, walk in him, rooted and built up in him, and established in the faith” (2:6–7). You do not need a second Saviour or a secret supplement. You need more of the One you already have.

themesMastered.title: The Cross That Cancelled the Debt and Defeated the Powers
themesMastered.body: The cross did two great things in Colossians. First, it dealt with our guilt: God was “wiping out the handwriting in ordinances which was against us; and he has taken it out of the way, nailing it to the cross” (2:14). The debt you could never repay has been cancelled, and the document is gone. Second, it dealt with the powers: “having stripped the principalities and the powers, he made a show of them openly, triumphing over them in it” (2:15). The spiritual forces the Colossians feared were led in Christ's victory parade. Believers do not need to appease or fear them; they need to stand in Christ, who has already won.

themesMastered.title: Raised With Christ: Put Off, Put On
themesMastered.body: “If then you were raised together with Christ, seek the things that are above, where Christ is, seated on the right hand of God” (3:1). Holiness in Colossians is not achieved by rules, which have no power against the flesh, but by union with Christ in His death and resurrection. You died, and your life is hidden with Him. So you put to death what belongs to the old life, put away anger, malice and lies, and put on the new self, being renewed in the image of the Creator. In that new humanity “Christ is all, and in all” (3:11). And over all the new garments you put on love, which holds everything together.

themesMastered.title: Everything in His Name
themesMastered.body: “Whatever you do, in word or in deed, do all in the name of the Lord Jesus, giving thanks to God the Father, through him” (3:17). The supremacy of Christ is not only a doctrine for theologians; it reaches into marriages, families and workplaces. Wives and husbands, children and fathers, servants and masters all live under the same Lord. Work becomes worship: “And whatever you do, work heartily, as for the Lord, and not for men” (3:23). Prayer, speech to unbelievers, friendships and ministries — all are lived in His name. Thanksgiving runs through the whole letter because a life lived for Christ is a grateful life.

experientialLesson.intro: How do you walk out the Book of Colossians practically moving forward? Here is your experiential blueprint:

steps.title: Look Again at Who He Is
steps.lesson: The Lesson: Paul's answer to the false teaching was not a list of arguments but a fresh vision of Christ: “who is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of all creation” (1:15). Most spiritual anxiety, confusion and drift begins with a small view of Jesus. When Christ is seen as He truly is, competing voices lose their pull.
steps.practice: The Practice: Copy out Colossians 1:15–20 by hand, line by line. Read it aloud every morning for a week. Each day, pick one phrase — ‘image of the invisible God’, ‘all things have been created through him’, ‘in him all things are held together’, ‘the head of the body’, ‘the firstborn from the dead’, ‘having made peace through the blood of his cross’ — and spend five minutes worshipping Christ for that one truth. At the end of the week, write down how your view of Him has grown and what fears or worries looked smaller because of it.

steps.title: Cross Out the Additions
steps.lesson: The Lesson: “For in him all the fullness of the Deity dwells bodily, and in him you are made full” (2:9–10). Every ‘Christ plus’ teaching robs believers of the joy and freedom of being complete in Him, and keeps them anxious, judging others or trying to earn what they already have.
steps.practice: The Practice: Write down anything you have felt you need, beyond Christ, to be fully accepted by God or to feel spiritually secure — a practice, an experience, a rule, a performance, a level of knowledge. Hold each item up to Colossians 2:9–15. Thank God for anything that is a good help in following Christ, but cross out anything you have been treating as an addition to Him. Then write over the page, ‘In him you are made full.’ Keep it where you will see it, especially when you feel spiritually inadequate.

steps.title: Live One Day Fully in His Name
steps.lesson: The Lesson: The supreme Christ is Lord of ordinary life. “Whatever you do, in word or in deed, do all in the name of the Lord Jesus” (3:17), and “whatever you do, work heartily, as for the Lord, and not for men” (3:23). Colossians refuses to divide life into sacred and secular.
steps.practice: The Practice: Choose one ordinary day and live it consciously in Christ's name. In the morning, read 3:1–4 and set your mind on Him. Before each task, say, ‘Lord, this is for You.’ At home, practise one of the instructions of 3:18–21. At work, serve heartily whether or not anyone is watching. In conversation, let your speech be gracious and seasoned with salt (4:6). Give thanks at every meal. In the evening, write down what changed. Then repeat the day once a week until it becomes the shape of your life.

finalDeclaration: “Father, I close this letter written by a prisoner about a King, and I declare: Jesus Christ is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of all creation. By Him all things were created — in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible, thrones and dominions, principalities and powers. All things were created through Him and for Him. He is before all things, and in Him all things hold together. He is the Head of the body, the church, the firstborn from the dead, and in everything He has the first place. All Your fullness dwells in Him bodily, and in Him I am made complete. I need nothing added to Him. I will not be carried off by empty philosophy or the traditions of men. As I received Christ Jesus the Lord, so I will walk in Him, rooted and built up in Him, established in the faith and overflowing with thanksgiving. I was dead in my trespasses, and You made me alive with Him and forgave me all my sins. The record of debt that stood against me was nailed to the cross. Every principality and power has been disarmed and put to open shame. I will not live under shadows when I have the substance. I have been raised with Christ, so I set my mind on the things above, where Christ is seated at Your right hand. My life is hidden with Christ in You, and when He appears I will appear with Him in glory. I put to death what belongs to my old life, and I put on the new self, renewed in His image. I clothe myself with compassion, kindness, humility, gentleness and patience, I forgive as He forgave me, and above all I put on love. The peace of Christ rules in my heart, and His word dwells in me richly. In my home and in my work, I serve the Lord Christ. I will continue steadfastly in prayer, walk in wisdom toward outsiders, and let my speech be full of grace. I will fulfil the ministry I have received in the Lord. Whatever I do, in word or deed, I will do it all in the name of the Lord Jesus, giving thanks to You through Him. Christ is all, and in all. In the mighty name of Jesus, Amen!”
